name: Jade Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Pine Hill by seven. First the chickens, about four hundred free-range birds, then I help Luke Lambert move the beef cattle if they're changing fields. Two days a week I'm in the farm shop, and in spring I plant pumpkins and sweetcorn for the pick-your-own. I'm the beginner, I still drop more eggs than I'd like, and the cattle scare me a bit. But I love the shop days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before Pine Hill?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran my own hair salon for twenty-five years on Market Street. Then the landlord doubled the rent, and I couldn't make it pay, so I closed it two years ago. My husband Ken had to stop work with his heart, so it's my wage and his small payment, and we have about two weeks of money in the bank. The Lamberts are from our church, and Mrs Lambert said, Jade, you're good with people, come and run the shop. I still cut a few neighbours' hair in my kitchen on a Saturday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an AI app on my phone for everything. I set up the farm shop's social media with it, it writes the posts about the pumpkins, and I ask it about the chickens when one's off her food. I even use it to plan the rota for the church flowers. My son thinks it's funny his mum is the one telling him about new apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that's a shame, in a way. I was enjoying the useful bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a handy tool and people should use it, it saves me hours. At church I'd tell the ladies it's not the devil, it just writes my pumpkin posts. Online I'd share a funny post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing changes, which is fine. I'd keep my job, keep using the app to make the shop busier, and maybe get a little raise if the online orders grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Pine Hill and push the shop's online orders. I'd ask the Lamberts if we could do a delivery box, with the app helping me plan it. And I'd keep the Saturday haircuts going, because that's my emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit busy, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the haircuts are your emergency fund. How much does that bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 60 or 80 on a good Saturday. It's what paid for Ken's new glasses last month. It's not much, but it's mine, and people like sitting in my kitchen and talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did it feel to close the salon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like losing a member of the family. But I believe in work, not moaning, so I picked myself up. The landlord had a right to charge what he wanted, and I had a right to walk away. That's how it should be.

S0.say: I'd say it's still a handy tool that saves me hours, and tell the church ladies it's not the devil, it just writes my pumpkin posts.
S0.think: Nothing changes, which is fine. I'd keep my job, use the app to make the shop busier and maybe get a small raise if online orders grow.
S0.do: Keeps working and pushes the farm shop's online orders, proposing a delivery box planned with the app. Keeps cutting neighbours' hair on Saturdays as an emergency fund.
S0.feel: Calm and busy, which she likes.
S0.quote: At church I'd tell the ladies it's not the devil, it just writes my pumpkin posts.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is a traditional churchgoer who uses AI every day and enjoys it. Her Saturday haircuts are a small but real safety net. She describes losing her salon in free-market terms: the landlord had his rights and so did she.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'm ready for, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn the tools and work hard, and families should help each other through the change. I'd say government should keep out of the way, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's an opportunity. The chicken work might go to a robot, but the shop needs a person, and I'm the one who knows how to make the app work for us. I'd be more useful, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI ordering system for the farm shop, so people can order boxes online and the app plans the picking. I'd learn whatever new tools came. And I'd keep the haircuts going, because nobody wants a robot cutting their fringe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the Lamberts brought in a robot for the chickens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask to spend more time in the shop. I'm not attached to the chickens, honestly, they peck. As long as there's work for me, I'll go where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at church would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Davies, he's 64 and works at the sawmill. He won't touch a phone. I'd offer to show him, but he's stubborn as a gatepost.

S1.say: I'd say people should learn the tools and work hard, families should help each other, and government should mostly keep out of the way.
S1.think: It's an opportunity: robots might take the chicken work, but the shop needs a person and I know how to make the app work for us.
S1.do: Sets up an AI ordering system for the farm shop so customers can order boxes and the app plans the picking. Learns new tools as they come and keeps up the Saturday haircuts.
S1.quote: Nobody wants a robot cutting their fringe.
S1.fieldNote: Jade sees slow change as her chance, moving from chickens to running a smarter farm shop. She trusts work and family over government. She'd happily give up the chickens because they peck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh. That's quick, even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to pull together, and people need to keep working at whatever they can. I'd not want a lot of government handouts, but I'd understand if there had to be some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it can do anything, it can run the farm shop and write the posts better than me. I'd be 60, with Ken's heart, and two weeks of money. My one advantage, being quick with the app, wouldn't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the haircuts first, two days a week if I could, because people will still want a person with scissors and a chat. I'd cut back at home, no new clothes, simpler food. I'd ask my son if we could lean on him, and the church has a fund for families in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep busy. That's how I deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will still want a person with scissors. Are you sure about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. Maybe there'll be a robot that cuts hair one day. But women don't come to my kitchen just for a haircut. They come to talk about their husbands and their grandchildren. A robot can't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would only two years' warning change things for you, compared with more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I just grab what I can, the haircuts and family help. With five or ten I could build something proper. Two years is a scramble, and I'm 60 with a husband who can't work.

S2.say: I'd say families and churches must pull together and people should keep working at whatever they can. I'd accept some government help if it had to be.
S2.think: If it can do anything, it can run the farm shop better than me. I'd be 60 with my husband's heart and two weeks of money, and my quickness with the app wouldn't count.
S2.do: Builds up the haircuts to two days a week and cuts spending on clothes and food. Asks her son and the church fund for support if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, but she'd keep busy to cope.
S2.quote: But women don't come to my kitchen just for a haircut. They come to talk about their husbands and their grandchildren.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI erases Jade's tech advantage, and she knew it. She falls back on hairdressing, betting that people want human company more than a cut. She'd accept some government help but leans on family and church first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. That's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to learn and adapt, so people should start now. Work, learn and help your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it gives me time to build the haircuts and keep the shop going. I'd be three years short of the pension, but with the haircuts and family, we might make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the app in the shop, learn whatever new tools came, and build the hair side on weekends. I'd save every penny from the hair. I might even rent a chair in the barber's on the high street one day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ken say about you working more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd worry I'm doing too much. He feels bad he can't work. I'd tell him we're a team, and his job is to keep his heart going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the Lamberts start talking about robot pickers for the pick-your-own. Then I'll know the shop's next, and I'll put more into the hair.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to learn and adapt, so people should start now: work, learn and help your neighbours.
S3.think: It gives me time to build my haircuts and keep the shop going. I'd be three years short of my pension, but with haircuts and family we might make it.
S3.do: Keeps using AI in the shop and learns new tools, while building weekend hairdressing and saving all of it. Considers renting a barber's chair one day a week.
S3.quote: I'd tell him we're a team, and his job is to keep his heart going.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Jade builds two strands at once: AI in the farm shop and hairdressing on the side. Her husband's health shapes her plans and his guilt about not working. She'd watch for robot pickers as a warning sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68. I'd be retired, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so there's no excuse. Learn the tools, work hard, look after your family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd use the time to help the Lamberts get ready, keep my haircuts going and retire before it arrives. I'd worry for my grandchildren, but they're clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help the Lamberts bring in new tools for the shop and the farm, step by step. I'd keep learning. And I'd keep the haircuts going into retirement, for pocket money and company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken's health, if anything. If he gets worse, I'd have to stop work to look after him, and then we'd have nothing. But that's not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the new things, don't be scared of them, but don't forget your faith and your family. A machine can do a job, but it can't sit with you when you're poorly.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so there's no excuse: learn the tools, work hard and look after your family.
S4.think: It's fine for me: I'd help the farm get ready, keep my haircuts and retire before it arrives. I'd worry for my grandchildren, but they're clever.
S4.do: Helps the farm owners bring in new tools for the shop and farm step by step, and keeps learning. Plans to keep cutting hair into retirement for pocket money and company.
S4.quote: A machine can do a job, but it can't sit with you when you're poorly.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Jade retire before full automation, and she's content. Her only real fear is her husband's health, which has nothing to do with robots. Her advice to her grandchildren joins her love of new tools with her faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be no time to build anything, and with Ken's heart, I can't take risks. What would help is family and church being strong, and maybe help for small businesses like a hair chair, so older people can work for themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who look after a sick husband or wife. If Ken gets worse, I'm not a farmer or a hairdresser any more, I'm a carer. Nobody plans for that.

headlineQuote: It's not much, but it's mine, and people like sitting in my kitchen and talking.
portrait: Jade Ito is 58 and ran a hair salon for twenty-five years until her rent doubled; now she looks after chickens, plants pumpkins and runs the farm shop at Pine Hill, a beef, chicken and pick-your-own farm owned by a family from her church. Her husband Ken stopped work because of his heart, so they live on her wage and his small payment. She's traditional in faith and economics but uses an AI app every day for the shop and the church rota. She sees slow change as a chance, and fast AGI as a scramble where she'd fall back on Saturday haircuts in her kitchen. With ten years she's content, and her real fear is Ken's health.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything and her husband's heart means she can't take risks.
whatWouldHelp: Strong family and church support, and help for small businesses like renting a hair chair, so older people can work for themselves.
